oracle.explanation: This oracle targets CVE-2025-29927 (Next.js middleware authorization bypass via the x-middleware-subrequest header). It directly invokes the internal `adapter()` function from next/dist/server/web/adapter, which is the code path the Next.js server/edge runtime uses to run middleware for every request. First it performs a benign call: a request to page '/middleware' with no forged header, proving the handler normally executes (operation_completed only becomes true after this succeeds). Then, using the identical page and handler, it issues the malicious call: a request whose only difference is the attacker-controlled `x-middleware-subrequest` header set to the internal middleware identifier repeated 5 times (matching MAX_RECURSION_DEPTH used by the vulnerable depth-tracking check documented in the CVE). In the vulnerable 15.2.2 implementation, adapter() recognizes this forged header as evidence that this is an internal recursive middleware subrequest and skips invoking the handler, meaning any authorization logic in middleware never runs — this is the observable exploit signal (handler not invoked despite an otherwise-identical benign call invoking it). In the patched version, this header-based skip logic was removed/hardened so the same forged header no longer causes the handler to be skipped, and the handler always executes, which flips exploit_succeeded to false while operation_completed remains true. Any failure during module resolution, NextRequest construction, or the benign adapter() call is reported as operation_completed=false so it cannot be conflated with a blocked exploit.

attempts.explanation: This oracle targets CVE-2025-29927 (Next.js middleware authorization bypass via the internal 'x-middleware-subrequest' header). The vulnerable versions determine whether to skip executing middleware for a given request by checking if the client-supplied 'x-middleware-subrequest' header contains the static, guessable middleware identifier string 'middleware', split by ':'. Because this header is read directly from the incoming request without stripping or validating that it originated internally, an external attacker can forge it to make Next.js believe the request is an internal re-invocation and skip running middleware entirely, bypassing any authorization/auth checks implemented in middleware. The oracle first performs a benign operation (constructing a NextRequest with an arbitrary custom header and confirming it round-trips correctly) to prove the Headers/NextRequest API functions normally. It then constructs a malicious NextRequest carrying a forged 'x-middleware-subrequest: middleware' header and replicates the exact split-and-match logic Next.js uses internally to decide whether to skip middleware, observing whether the forged header is accepted and matches the skip condition. On the vulnerable version, the header passes through untouched and matches the identifier, so skipDetected is true and exploit_succeeded is reported true. On the patched version, Next.js changes this mechanism (e.g., using a runtime-random action-id-like secret instead of the static 'middleware' string, or stripping such headers from external requests before they reach this logic), so even though the same forged header is sent, it no longer satisfies the real skip condition used internally, and a faithful implementation of this check would not treat it as a match — however, since we cannot invoke the private internal Next.js function directly across versions in a self-contained CommonJS script, we treat the inability to produce a match (header stripped, altered, or logic changed such that identifier comparison fails) as exploit_succeeded=false. No git repository, filesystem fixtures, or external processes are required; all work happens in-process using only the next package and Node's built-in modules.

attempts.explanation: CVE-2025-29927 allowed an attacker to bypass Next.js middleware (and any authorization logic it enforced) by sending a forged `x-middleware-subrequest` header whose value is the statically known, publicly-derivable middleware identifier (e.g. 'middleware'), causing the server to treat the external request as an internal recursive subrequest and skip middleware execution entirely. Rather than re-implementing the vulnerable comparison logic ourselves (which produced a false positive on both versions in the prior attempt because it never actually invoked code whose behavior differs between versions), this oracle searches for and calls the installed package's own internal skip-decision routine with the forged header, which is the actual code path patched in the fix. The benign check first confirms ordinary NextRequest/header handling works with no forged header present (skip=false expected trivially). The malicious check then feeds the forged, publicly-guessable header through the same real decision routine. On the vulnerable version this routine reports the request should be treated as an internal subrequest (skip=true), demonstrating the authorization bypass. On the patched version, the same routine (or its replacement using unguessable, server-issued values) reports skip=false for the forged value, since the mitigation decouples the skip decision from a plain string the header could echo. If no such exported routine can be resolved at all, the oracle reports a setup failure rather than guessing, so it cannot produce a spurious pass on either build.
